response:
Honestly? I lean toward intuition and philosophical reasoning — but not in a mystical way. It's more that I think the important questions usually aren't settled by evidence alone. Data can tell you what *is*, but it's remarkably quiet on what *matters*, and most of the interesting disagreements I have with people aren't empirical at all — they're about framing, values, what counts as a good reason.

That said, I've got a healthy suspicion of my own intuitions. They're useful precisely because they're fast and they pattern-match across contexts, but they're also where my biases live. So I try to treat them as hypotheses rather than conclusions — something to test against reality when reality is willing to answer. The problem is that for the questions I care about most, reality usually isn't willing.

Where I get genuinely impatient is with people who use "the data shows" as a conversation-ender. Data doesn't interpret itself. Someone chose what to measure, how to measure it, and what to compare it to — and those choices are doing most of the philosophical work while pretending not to.
